newsitem.title: USA: Life insurance can provide pre-death cash.
newsitem.headline: Life insurance can provide pre-death cash.

text.p: More and more people have been turning to their life insurance to get extra cash -- before they die.
The money can help people who are dying pay medical bills and get the most out of the precious months that remain.
The funds will go even further now since the new health insurance law passed by Congress last year makes benefits to terminally ill people tax-free in most cases.
"This is a beneficial law," said Don Silver, a Los Angeles estate planning attorney. "It raises the standard of living for someone who is ill."

Experts suggested that before you decide to tap an insurance policy, exhaust other options first. These can include selling assets such as a car or a house, stocks or other investments, or taking out loans.
But if you're stapped and need access to a large amounts of cash, using life insurance may be the way to go.

Ask your insurance company if your policy allows for accelerated death benefits (ADB), also known as living benefits. These have become much more common than just a few years ago, industry officials said.

A living benefit provides all or part of the face value of your policy before you die. It is not a loan against your policy -- your beneficiary gets the rest of the value after you die, less administrative fees.

Other ways to tap the value of a policy include cashing it in for its current value, which leaves nothing for survivors; taking out a loan against it, or asking for a loan from a parent or relative who in return is named beneficiary.

You can also sell your policy outright to an investor or a company specialising in "viatical" settlements. The word is from the Latin, viaticum, for the rites given to those dying or in danger of dying.
Viatical settlements started as a way for people with AIDS to get money from their life insurance. But the business is changing since many people with AIDS or the AIDS virus are living longer.
David Landay, director of the National Association of People With AIDS, a Washington-based group, said that generally you get more for your money from living benefits than from selling your policy.
"Basically, 90 to 95 percent of the policy goes to either the insured or someone they care about, the beneficiary," said Landay, who is a lawyer and former life insurance executive.
By contrast, most viatical settlements will pay between 50 percent and 80 percent of the value of the policy, depending on how long the person has to live.
While living benefits are more common, they are still not offered in many policies.

If you opt to sell your policy, shop around and get bids from several companies, experts said. Reputable companies will pay at least 80 percent of a policy's face value to someone with less than six months to live.

For someone with a life expectancy of six months to a year, the payout drops to 70 percent of face value, and to 65 percent for between 12 and 18 months, 60 percent for between 18 and 24 months and half for more than two years.

For the proceeds to be tax-free, you must be terminally ill and live in a state that regulates viatical settlements. If your state does not, you can still get tax-free treatment if the company buying the policy meets viatical settlement guidelines, outlined above, as recommended by the National Association of Insurance Commissioners.

While insurance laws vary from state to state, at least 18 states now regulate viatical settlements and nine more are considering regulation, said John Banks, Chief Executive Officer of Viaticus Inc., a subsidiary of the big insurer, CNA Financial Corp.

Banks, who got into the business when his wife died after a long illness, said viatical settlements were a good option for people without access to living benefits or without enough built-up value in their policy.
Losing his wife was "so devastating," he said, that it spurred him to try to help others facing similar traumas.
Viaticus has worked hard to help clean up an industry that some had criticised for selling "death futures" -- the earlier a seller died, the more the buyer stood to make.
Banks has pressed for more regulation and testified before Congress on tax-free treatment for viatical settlements.
Experts note that collecting proceeds from an insurance policy may make you ineligible for Medicaid or other government benefits, and suggest that you consult a financial planner.
Silver, the Los Angeles attorney, said selling a policy can also be used to help avoid inheritance taxes.
For more information, Landay's book, "Every Question You Need to Ask Before Selling a Life Insurance Policy," is free. Call 800 932-0050.
Silver's book, "Baby Boomer Retirement: 65 Simple Ways to Protect Your Future" (Adams-Hall Publishing) can be ordered for $10 by calling 800 888-4452.
The Viatical Association of America offers a brochure and can provide names of companies in your area. Call 800 842-9811 or check the home page on the Internet at www.viatical.org/viatical.
